canonical_statement: The authors interpreted the paired concentration pattern as asynchronous elimination of cabotegravir and rilpivirine after prolonged injection delays, consistent with the longer literature-reported apparent elimination half-life of long-acting rilpivirine (13–28 weeks) than cabotegravir (6–12 weeks).

The authors stated that no physiologically based pharmacokinetic modeling or population pharmacokinetic simulations had specifically addressed the prolonged missed-injection scenario described in this series.

The authors proposed that the disproportionate cabotegravir decline could create suboptimal and unbalanced exposure with a transient state of functional monotherapy, raising a theoretical risk of resistance selection despite no virological failure in the four cases.

The authors cautioned against direct comparison with prior cabotegravir tail-phase data because study populations, clinical settings, and pharmacokinetic assessment approaches differed, and they noted interindividual variability in long-acting cabotegravir pharmacokinetics.

The authors concluded that the case series provides real-world evidence of differential pharmacokinetic decay between cabotegravir and rilpivirine after missed injections; virological suppression was maintained in all cases, but the potential for transient functional monotherapy warrants further investigation.
The study was carried out as part of the authors’ routine work.
